one_liner: Pure-Rust, no_std big-integer crate (an ibig fork) that beats GMP via rug on one- and two-word values.
what_it_does: dashu-int provides UBig and IBig arbitrary-precision integers with operator overloading, pow, gcd/gcd_ext, roots, logarithms, base 2-36 parsing and printing, ConstDivisor for repeated division by an invariant, and Montgomery modular arithmetic (monty::MontgomeryRepr) for odd moduli. It is one crate of the dashu family (also floats, decimals, rationals and complex numbers) that aims to be a Rust-native alternative to GMP, MPFR and MPC. The API is idiomatic Rust, not mpz-compatible; C++ code can reach it only through a hand-written FFI layer.
how_it_is_fast: The internal Repr is a union that stores one- or two-word magnitudes inline (up to 128 bits on 64-bit targets) and only spills to the heap above that, so small values never allocate, while GMP via rug pays a heap allocation per value; 0.6.1 also copies inline values directly on clone and compares them as single words. Larger operands use schoolbook multiplication with a double-word addmul kernel (BMI2 mulx on x86-64 with std), Karatsuba, Toom-3 from 96 words and, since 0.4.3, Proth-prime NTT with Garner CRT above about 4,000 words; division is schoolbook plus divide-and-conquer, and gcd is Lehmer's algorithm.
when_to_use: Rust code where most integers fit in 128 bits but must not overflow (checked accumulators, parsers, symbolic or property-testing workloads): at 100 bits the report shows add 3.7 vs 21.9 ns and div 5.7 vs 32.4 ns against rug/GMP.
no_std or WebAssembly targets, or projects that cannot link LGPL GMP: it is pure Rust under MIT OR Apache-2.0.
Hex parsing and gcd around 1000 bits, where dashu matched or beat rug in the report (gcd 2.87 vs 3.05 us; from_hex at 10^4 bits 2.56 vs 6.60 us).
When you need integers, rationals, decimals and binary floats from one consistent pure-Rust family.
when_not_to_use: Operands of about 1000 bits and up: rug/GMP wins add, sub, mul, div, pow and modular arithmetic there (mul at 10^4 bits 4.52 vs 12.76 us; modular pow at 1000 bits 305 vs 771 us).

Large-number workloads such as computing many digits of a constant: in tczajka/bigint-benchmark-rs, 10M digits of e take 19.9 s with dashu 0.4.2 vs 2.8 s with rug, and Fibonacci(100M) 26.2 s vs 2.9 s.
C++ projects: there is no C API, so using it from C++ means writing and maintaining Rust FFI shims; a C++ small-value library such as mp++ or Boost.Multiprecision cpp_int is simpler.
Constant-time cryptography: no constant-time guarantees are documented (an optional zeroize feature exists, but that only clears memory).

integration.dependencies: dashu-base, cfg-if, static_assertions, num-modular; optional num-order (default), num-traits, num-integer, rand, serde, zeroize, rkyv
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.68 (MSRV for the default build; some optional features such as rkyv_v08 need Rust 1.81+)
integration.platforms: any Rust target (16-, 32- and 64-bit words); BMI2 mulx kernel on x86-64 with std; NTT multiplication compiled out on smaller-word targets
integration.thread_safety: not documented; UBig and IBig are owned value types with no shared internal state

gotchas: The benchmark measured dashu-int 0.4.2, but the current release is 0.6.1; 0.4.3 added NTT multiplication, Montgomery arithmetic and lower Toom-3 thresholds, so large-operand gaps to GMP may now be smaller, and the small-value numbers have not been re-measured.

Versions before 0.4.3 could exhaust the scratch allocator in modular exponentiation for Karatsuba-sized moduli and panic in gcd_ext when one operand divides the other; before 0.5.1, gcd of two large similar-sized integers could abort with 'not enough memory allocated'. Use 0.5.1 or later.
0.5.0 changed IBig's serde binary format to two's-complement little-endian bytes, so data serialized by earlier versions does not deserialize.

The small-value win is mostly about allocation: each benchmarked op returns a new value, so rug pays a heap allocation while dashu stays inline; the 100-bit div bench divides operands of equal bit length, so it measures overhead rather than long division.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick dashu over ibig (its ancestor) because it keeps two words inline and has a much faster gcd (10^4 bits: 64 us vs 851 us), and over Malachite when you need a permissive license instead of LGPL or want the float, decimal and rational crates; pick Malachite for better large-operand speed, and blip_mp or ctbignum only outside Rust.
verified_claims_summary: DRMacIver/rust-bigint-benchmarks ran Criterion microbenchmarks (rustc 1.92.0, default bench profile, 2 s measurements) on an Apple M2 Max comparing dashu-int 0.4.2 with rug 1.30.0 (GMP via gmp-mpfr-sys 1.7.1) and other Rust crates: dashu was faster than rug in 98 of 153 small-value cases (e.g. 100-bit add 3.7 vs 21.9 ns), but rug won most cases from about 1000 bits upward. The report calls its numbers quick, machine-specific and not authoritative.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-30, 0.6.1 released 2026-09-25, about 3.9 million crates.io downloads), dual MIT/Apache-2.0, pre-1.0 with occasional breaking changes between minor versions.
